title: Phineas Gage (1848)

youtube.title: An Iron Rod Went Through His Head. He Lived. #Shorts
youtube.description:
1848, Vermont. A railroad foreman packs explosive powder with an iron rod. One spark, and the rod shoots straight through his skull.
Minutes later, he's sitting up and talking.

This is the real story of Phineas Gage, neuroscience's most famous patient, told from the inside. His friends said he was 'no longer Gage'. But many of the wild details came much later, and his years driving stagecoaches in Chile suggest his brain partly adapted.

If your brain can change who you are, who is the real YOU? Tell me in the comments.

Sources:
- Harlow, J. M. (1868). Recovery from the passage of an iron bar through the head. Publications of the Massachusetts Medical Society, 2, 327-347.
- Macmillan, M. (2000). An Odd Kind of Fame: Stories of Phineas Gage. MIT Press.
- Macmillan, M., & Lena, M. L. (2010). Rehabilitating Phineas Gage. Neuropsychological Rehabilitation, 20(5), 641-658.

sources: Harlow (1848, 1868): on 13 September 1848 near Cavendish, Vermont, a tamping iron about 3 ft 7 in (about 1.1 m) long and about 13 pounds shot up through Gage's left cheek and out the top of his head and landed some distance behind him; he spoke within minutes and greeted the doctor (Edward Williams) with 'here is business enough for you'.
Harlow (1868): his friends and acquaintances said he was 'no longer Gage'. Gage died in May 1860, almost twelve years after the accident.
Macmillan (2000) and Macmillan & Lena (2010): many later accounts exaggerated his changes; he worked for years as a stagecoach driver in Chile, suggesting substantial recovery.
lines: You're a railroad foreman in Vermont. In one second, an iron rod will shoot straight through your head. And you'll survive.
Eighteen forty-eight. Your crew blasts rock for a new railroad. Your job: pack explosive powder into a hole with an iron rod.
A spark. The powder explodes. The rod, over a metre long, flies up through your cheek and out the top of your skull.
It lands far behind you. Minutes later, you're sitting up, talking. You tell the doctor: here is business enough for you.
Your body heals. But your doctor later writes that your friends say something strange: you are no longer Gage.
About thirteen pounds of iron went through the front of your brain. And you lived for almost twelve more years.
But textbooks often turn you into a monster. Many of those wild details were added long after you died.
In fact, you spent years in Chile driving a stagecoach. Horses, mountain roads, passengers. That takes planning and self-control.
Your brain changed you, and then it may have adapted. If your brain can change who you are, who is the real you?
